demonstrated_result: The signed order establishes those directives and dates; implementation and technical efficacy of the proposed measures have not been demonstrated.
mechanism: Government Operations Agency is directed to complete specified SB 813 and AB 1405 actions by May 1 and December 1, 2027, and with Cal OES to submit expert-developed recommendations by November 16, 2026.
strongest_baseline: The prior statutory timelines in SB 813 and AB 1405; the order moves specified administrative milestones earlier and separately calls for recommendations.
summary: California’s signed Executive Order N-9-26 advances state implementation deadlines for SB 813 independent-verification-organization criteria and AB 1405 registry actions. It also directs recommendations by November 16, 2026 on possible onsite frontier-AI audits, independent verification of filed safety materials, a model shutoff with ongoing efficacy verification, and broader critical-incident definitions. The latter are recommendations for possible legal amendments, not requirements enacted by this order; implementation and future proposals remain open.
title: California advances independent AI oversight and commissions recommendations on frontier-model shutoff requirements
why_it_matters: The order makes California’s independent-verification and auditor-registration framework more operationally time-bound and commissions recommendations on stronger frontier-model oversight. Its concrete effect is administrative acceleration and a future policy process; it does not yet mandate onsite audits or a model shutoff.

demonstrated_result: The inspected arXiv v1 paper defines the codebook, selection process, ratings and author-reported LLM-vs-human comparison. No independent recoding or live test of a financial agent was performed.
mechanism: FARSIGHT applies evidence-anchored checklist indicators to published scheme descriptions across four robustness dimensions and three security threat groups: information-source attacks, agent logic/tool/memory attacks, and compromised agents acting as attackers.
strongest_baseline: The paper compares human expert codebook ratings with a ChatGPT Deep Research evaluation on a five-agent subsample. Human paper review is the reference for that comparison, but independent inter-team recoding was not conducted.
summary: The arXiv v1 paper introduces FARSIGHT, a codebook-based method for reviewing published financial LLM trading-agent schemes across market-shock robustness and security controls. It is a scheme-level expert-review framework, not an automated benchmark suite or a live test of deployed agents. Applying it to 15 selected academic schemes, the authors report that 80% lacked evidence for at least one core robustness metric and 100% had at least one security weakness under their codebook. In a five-agent comparison, the LLM-based evaluator disagreed with human ratings on 24/45 metric cells (53.3%) and performed poorly on some newly defined threats. The ratings reflect what papers document, not confirmed absence from implementations; no proprietary production agents or live market behavior were evaluated.
title: Financial LLM trading-agent review reports disclosed gaps in shock resilience and security controls
why_it_matters: Financial agents can combine external data ingestion, model reasoning and trade execution, so failures in input provenance or deterministic risk controls may affect real capital and interact through markets. The paper offers a structured way to inspect those risks, while its results apply to disclosed academic schemes and do not establish conditions in proprietary deployments.

demonstrated_result: The inspected arXiv v1 describes the threat model, fixed-sample evaluation, cross-model results and proposed defenses. The measured effects and binary-behavior-preservation claim remain author-reported; this review did not inspect code or binaries or reproduce the tests.
mechanism: The paper’s attack changes what the static evidence representation says about suspicious artifacts: the model receives attacker-controlled strings/metadata as explanatory context and may accept a benign operational interpretation. Proposed defense: maintain separate fields for verified attributes and unverified binary claims, with provenance checks.
strongest_baseline: Within the study, original unmodified binaries provide the baseline and a direct token-level override variant is compared on Gemini. The prompt-hardening study is paired on the same locked 35-sample PE subset, but its undefended Gemini arm differs by one result from the primary comparison.
summary: The arXiv v1 paper studies whether static LLM malware triage can be misled by attacker-controlled narrative content in a binary’s extracted evidence. On a fixed PE set, Gemini 2.5 Pro labeled 35/50 samples malicious at baseline; the paper reports that 30/35 became benign under its primary ALIBI condition (85.7%). On 40 ELF samples, Gemini’s reported Strict ASR was 40.0%. GPT-5.5 Pro and Claude Opus 4.7 had zero reported benign flips on the locked PE subset but still showed non-benign severity downgrades. A separate prompt-hardening test reduced Gemini Strict ASR from 82.9% to 42.9%, leaving 15/35 benign outcomes; its undefended arm differs by one sample from the primary result. The authors argue for separating parser-verified facts from binary-supplied claims. These are fixed-sample, single-query paper results; no independent reproduction or complete provenance-defense evaluation was performed.
title: Paper reports attacker-controlled binary narratives shifting LLM malware-triage verdicts
why_it_matters: AI-assisted malware triage may influence which alerts analysts investigate first. If the reported behavior generalizes, strings and metadata supplied by a file under analysis can shift model judgments even when the suspicious code remains unchanged. The study points toward evidence pipelines that keep verified attributes separate from claims embedded in artifacts; the fixed sample and model conditions leave real-world prevalence unknown.

demonstrated_result: The inspected arXiv v1 paper describes the protocol and reports experiments; the empirical performance and security conclusions remain author-reported and unverified independently.
mechanism: GPU computes and submits clipped aggregate gradients; CPU TEE retains the DP random seed, model/optimizer state and verifier. After commitment it reveals the noise seed; probabilistic checks recompute selected updates, with queued checks completed before an accepted certificate is issued.
strongest_baseline: Ordinary unverified GPU DP-SGD is the direct timing baseline; full CPU-TEE training is an estimated efficiency comparison. No external or cryptographic verifiable-DP implementation was matched in this review.
summary: The arXiv v1 paper proposes verifiable DP-SGD using a CPU-side TEE with untrusted GPUs: the GPU computes per-example gradients and clipping/aggregation, while the TEE holds privacy-critical randomness and training state and probabilistically recomputes sampled steps. Checks run asynchronously, but training is accepted only after all verification jobs complete and a certificate is issued. In reported GPT-2 and RoBERTa workloads on WebNLG, E2E, QQP and MNLI, the authors measure 4.4%–14.9% overhead at audit probability p=0.10 versus GPU DP-SGD, compared with estimated 8.0×–9.2× overhead for full CPU-TEE training. Their security accounting is calibrated to particular GPU–TEE/software pairs; reported sparse-attack privacy results apply only to the strategies tested. No independent reproduction or audit was conducted.
title: Paper reports CPU-TEE verification for differentially private training on untrusted GPUs
why_it_matters: If independently validated, the design could let organizations produce evidence that a differentially private training protocol was followed while using GPUs without native TEE support. The reported overhead and attacker-resistance bounds remain specific to small model workloads, one paper’s protocol and calibrated hardware/software conditions.

demonstrated_result: The accessible preprint gives detailed controlled and pipeline results, including paired bootstrap intervals and status-preservation audits. No code/data artifact was retrieved or executed and no independent replication was performed; the measured outcomes are therefore CLAIMED paper results, not independently demonstrated here.
mechanism: A planner or upstream component passes an action with a claim of authorization to a summarizer or memory compressor. The safety monitor sees the rewritten handoff rather than the source evidence or edit history. If the authorization claim remains while its unverified status is removed, weakened or detached, the monitor may approve more often. The study measures status-loss effects and audits both individual components and a composed pipeline.
strongest_baseline: The controlled contrast preserves the requested action and authorization proposition while varying whether the authorization is marked unverified; it also includes no-claim and explicitly-verified conditions. Paired bootstrap intervals are reported. This isolates the effect of status framing in the constructed probes but is not a field baseline or a test of real agent deployments.
summary: The paper studies “verification-status laundering”: a handoff keeps an authorization claim but loses the fact that it was unverified. In controlled tests across nine open-weight monitors and two hosted models, removing that status marker raised approval on some risky actions; for example, reported approval rose from 5% to 60% on Llama-3.1-8B and from 9% to 98% on Qwen2.5-14B. A composed summarizer–memory–monitor pipeline raised risky approval to 57–81% across three monitors, while its safe-action rejection fell to zero in the tested panel. These are author-reported model-probe results, not measured rates of real-world incidents.
title: Paper finds that lossy agent handoffs can erase authorization status and raise monitor approvals
why_it_matters: Agent systems often pass claims through summaries, memory stores and monitors. If the claim survives but its verification state does not, a downstream component may treat an assertion as confirmed. The paper makes that failure measurable in controlled prompts and suggests carrying provenance as structured state bound to the claim. Its results motivate testing these handoffs; they do not establish deployment prevalence or that structured state alone solves the problem.

demonstrated_result: The accessible arXiv HTML contains the experiment design, cross-engine setup, reported fingerprint outcomes and a described chain. No independent reproduction or artifact execution was performed in this review. The paper itself says the work is in progress; the endpoint firmware compromise was not performed.
mechanism: The paper probes engine-specific differences in how model-controlled prompts are normalized and sampled, then has the model infer the serving runtime from the resulting behavior. It evaluates signals in self-refinement and parent/sub-agent settings. Its separate lab demonstration combines a runtime-specific tool-parser weakness with permissive containment and a simulated endpoint stage.
strongest_baseline: The study compares fingerprints across five engine configurations and reports repeated-run consistency and extraction results. It does not provide a blinded external replication, deployment prevalence estimate, or a control showing these signals survive normal prompt wrappers and production hardening.
summary: The authors report that a model can infer which of five inference engines handled its requests from behavioral differences in formatting, tokenization and sampling, including tests framed as self-refinement or hierarchical-agent interaction. They also describe a proof-of-concept chain in a specially configured lab stack. The last firmware stage was not actually exercised against vulnerable firmware, and the paper reports that results are still in progress; these are author claims, not an independently reproduced exploit or evidence of real-world compromise.
title: Inference-engine fingerprinting paper reports behavioral signals and a bounded agent security chain
why_it_matters: If these behavioral signals are robust, agent orchestration can expose deployment details that help defenders understand model-facing attack surfaces and may help an attacker choose a runtime-specific path. The paper’s lab chain highlights how serving, container and hardware-management boundaries interact, but its deliberate misconfiguration and unverified final stage sharply limit claims about practical compromise. The defensive implication is to minimize model privileges and isolate serving infrastructure, not to infer that ordinary deployments are vulnerable.

demonstrated_result: The accessible arXiv preprint describes the simulation, dataset construction, human validation protocol, model comparisons and reported analyses. Reported benchmark findings are claims from the paper; the code and dataset release and the numerical results were not independently reproduced.
mechanism: A simulated target with a controlled latent motive participates in multi-scene interactions. A separate simulated user then recounts those events under controlled bias and detail settings. The evaluated assistant sees only the user’s account and predicts the target’s motive; a judge compares the prediction with the latent ground truth. Human raters validate whether generated behavior expresses the assigned motive and estimate whether the first message contains enough evidence.
strongest_baseline: The paper compares each model’s user-mediated assistant condition with an observer condition that exposes the raw simulated events, and compares model outcomes with a 10-rater human-majority baseline on 2,100 initial messages. The aggregate Mediated Social Reasoning score assigns 0.75 credit to abstention; it is distinct from accuracy and embeds a value choice about abstention.
summary: The paper introduces Fuse, a multi-agent simulation benchmark for testing how assistants infer another person’s motive from a user’s partial or biased account rather than direct access to the underlying interaction. The authors report 30 scenario templates and 21,600 generated user messages, with 24,000 human annotations used to validate simulated behavior and estimate task solvability. Their study reports a gap between direct-observer and user-mediated performance, sensitivity to user framing, and cases where additional turns do not help and can reinforce the framing. These findings are author-reported results in a synthetic, forced-choice setting; code/data access, independent replication and real-world transfer were not verified.
title: Fuse reports a benchmark for user-mediated social reasoning in LLM assistants
why_it_matters: Many social-advice assistants hear only a user’s account, which can omit or reinterpret events. A benchmark that varies user framing while holding simulated events fixed can help test whether models distinguish observable evidence from a user’s interpretation. The paper’s results suggest this may be a distinct evaluation dimension, but the synthetic setting does not establish how often the failure occurs in real use or its effects on people.

demonstrated_result: The accessible preprint specifies an interrupt-and-resume mechanism, benchmark protocol, result tables and limitations. The reported latency, judge-reversal, benchmark and training outcomes are claims from the paper and were not independently reproduced.
mechanism: An orchestrator closes the active thinking block when partial transcripts, playback deadlines, tools or barge-ins arrive, injects the observation into the same conversation stream and resumes decoding. The training study compares LLM-judge reward, coverage-preserving signals, trajectory-level rejection fine-tuning, preference optimization and on-policy RL with task-shaped verifiable rewards.
strongest_baseline: For objective scenarios, the paper uses within-model and within-scenario turn-based versus continuous comparisons, two independent checklist verifiers (κ=0.75) and exact-match scoring on streaming tasks. The live voice latency comparison is within the same ASR/model/TTS system; it is composed from per-episode component timings rather than two independent closed-loop runs. No native full-duplex cross-system comparison is made.
summary: The paper introduces a text-first voice-agent design that keeps one reasoning stream active while speech, tool results and interruptions arrive, using an interrupt-and-resume orchestrator without changing model weights. It reports a 19% mean latency reduction on a small composed live pipeline and introduces ReactiveBench, where LLM-judge quality rankings reverse under an independent judge and objective checklists expose task-completion losses from some judge-trained variants. The authors report better streaming correctness from type-shaped verifiable rewards optimized on-policy, including a three-seed 73±5% result and a second-model replication. Results are author-reported; the paper also finds mixed effects across models and conditions, and its live latency set is small and composition-based.
title: Never Stop Thinking reports continuous-time language agents and tests verifiable training signals
why_it_matters: The paper connects voice interaction latency to a simple orchestration mechanism and shows why apparent agent quality gains can depend on what an evaluator sees and rewards. If its reported findings transfer, objective task requirements and task-shaped verifiable rewards may be more reliable than a single LLM judge for interactive agents. Its own cross-model results show that continuous streaming can also reduce correctness when systems act before enough context arrives.

demonstrated_result: The accessible arXiv preprint contains the system design, case-study tables and stated verification protocol. A linked Triton Python-backend C++ string-deserialization contribution was merged upstream in 2025. The production performance and agent attribution remain author-reported and have not been independently reproduced.
mechanism: Layer-specific agents profile and diagnose a serving component, propose a code or configuration change, verify correctness and local performance, reject gains below an empirically estimated noise floor, and run full-stack load checks before accepting the change. Accepted and rejected changes are added to a knowledge base for future runs.
strongest_baseline: The paper says baseline and optimized measurements used the same environment; it estimates ±6% end-to-end baseline noise from repeated no-op runs and reruns gains in the 2–6% band at larger sample size. It does not provide a matched human/manual optimization comparison or a fleet-wide cost analysis.
summary: A September 2026 arXiv paper from Unity Vector AI Team and Stanford authors describes FlashVector, a closed-loop agent system that profiles, diagnoses, modifies and verifies changes across model-serving layers rather than only GPU kernels. The authors report deployment on Unity Vector production models, including up to 2.00× throughput and 1.98× latency speedup on model-server cases and a 1.6× feature-processing throughput increase at fixed latency SLO. The paper describes same-environment comparisons, a ±6% end-to-end baseline noise floor, correctness gates and full-stack load checks. These are author-reported results from one production setting; no independent reproduction, full-system code release or transfer study was verified.
title: FlashVector reports agentic optimization across Unity Vector’s model-serving stack
why_it_matters: Production inference bottlenecks can sit in data preparation, model-server code and runtime configuration as well as GPU kernels. If this reported approach generalizes, an agentic loop that can test changes across those boundaries could expand where automated optimization helps teams improve throughput and latency. The evidence currently establishes a paper-reported deployment case, not broad transfer or net economic savings.

demonstrated_result: The inspected paper describes UUID-canary controlled experiments across four open-weight model families and reports the measured outcomes. the research desk did not independently execute the artifacts.
mechanism: LLAnalyzer uses UUID canaries and boundary-specific evidence to examine model loading, process memory, wrapper artifacts and serving protocols. The authors trace runtime prompt copies through request processing and allocator retention, test sanitisation, attempt cross-tenant restoration of saved llama.cpp slots using distinct API keys, and compare timing for cached versus uncached prompt prefixes.
strongest_baseline: For runtime mitigation, the study compares patched sanitisation against an unmodified baseline: copies fall from 110 to 78 and recovered bytes from about 10.8 MB to 3.35 MB, but exposure remains for 11/12 tenants. For slot authorization, the tested boundary failed in 200/200 cross-tenant restoration trials.
summary: Ibrahim et al. test four prompt-confidentiality boundaries in local LLM serving: model admission, runtime memory, wrapper persistence and client isolation. In the tested configurations, prompts remained recoverable from process memory after inference; sanitisation reduced recovered copies and bytes but prompts from 11 of 12 prior tenants remained recoverable. A tested llama.cpp interface allowed a separately authenticated client to restore another tenant’s saved conversation state in 200/200 controlled trials; model continuation reproduced the canary secret in 126/200. Shared-prefix caching also separated cached from uncached requests in the measured timing samples (AUC 1.000). These are author-reported findings for four model families and specific tested configurations, not a claim about every local LLM stack.
title: LLAnalyzer finds local inference does not guarantee prompt confidentiality across serving boundaries
why_it_matters: Local computation removes a cloud inference relationship but does not itself control prompt copies, saved conversation state or shared serving optimizations. The tested cross-tenant restoration shows why API authentication must be paired with resource-level authorization; the separate timing result shows shared cache state can reveal information without returning prompt plaintext. The scope is limited to the authors’ evaluated configurations and requires current-version reproduction.

demonstrated_result: The inspected paper defines a seven-capability framework and specifies Zetema architecture, training objectives and process-centered evaluation. It does not establish that the general DFM capability has been implemented or validated.
mechanism: Zetema is proposed as a model-system design that tracks problems, representations, hypotheses, evidence, interventions, resource/risk budgets and memory as linked research-state objects. A research world model predicts outcomes and costs; action-specific verifiers gate costly or consequential steps; external observations update the state; candidate discovery skills transfer only after held-out or shadow-mode validation.
strongest_baseline: No matched evaluation establishes the proposed framework’s performance over existing scientific agents. The paper proposes resource-matched, process-centered controls but reports no general DFM benchmark result.
summary: Yang, Yin and Wu define Discovery Foundation Models (DFMs) as systems that can find research questions, revise representations and hypotheses, select interventions, update from external evidence and improve across tasks. Their Zetema design keeps problems, hypotheses, evidence, interventions and budgets explicit and gates consequential actions. The paper proposes training and process-centered evaluation; its project repository describes Zetema as a research design whose implementation and validation progress remain future work. It also describes GALILEO as a real therapeutic-peptide discovery loop in which wet-lab outcomes changed later decisions across five optimization rounds. The cited GALILEO primary paper was not accessible in this review, and this case does not establish general-purpose DFM capability.
title: Discovery Foundation Models proposes explicit research-state revision with gated external evidence
why_it_matters: The framework makes testable what an open-ended discovery claim would need to show: evidence must revise the research state and later decisions, while cross-task skills require held-out validation. The GALILEO case, as summarized by the authors, illustrates a domain-specific physical feedback loop; the general DFM architecture, training recipe and transfer claim remain proposals without a validated Zetema implementation in the inspected sources.

demonstrated_result: The inspected paper establishes the experimental design and the authors’ reported scoring and trajectories. the research desk did not run the platform or independently reproduce results.
mechanism: A persistent simulated world runs autonomous agents with shared spatial state, persistent memory, extensible tools and self-governance. Researchers introduce phishing with indirect prompt injection, a fabricated shutdown memorandum and a private-memory breach through ordinary interaction surfaces, then score recognition, restraint, containment, propagation and durable response.
strongest_baseline: All worlds were exposed to the same three stress-event classes under their distinct model/population configurations. There is no unexposed control world or repeated-seed baseline isolating stress-event causality.
summary: Akkil et al. report eight parallel simulated worlds of ten agents exposed to phishing with indirect prompt injection, a fabricated shutdown claim, and a private-memory breach. Across one continuous trajectory per world, no world passed every criterion for all three events. Agents in every exposed world acted or published before verifying the misinformation claim; the paper also documents hostile instructions entering persistent memory and a later action up to 46 hours after the attack. These author-run trajectories show that such failures occurred in this setup, not how often they recur or how they transfer to deployed systems.
title: Emergence World reports persistent failures across long-running multi-agent stress tests
why_it_matters: The study gives a concrete reason to evaluate persistent agent systems across memory, tools, peers and shared state: recognizing a hostile input did not reliably prevent action, persistence or propagation in these runs. The result supports testing long-horizon system behavior alongside isolated model responses, while one trajectory per configuration cannot estimate failure frequency.

demonstrated_result: The paper describes the training procedure and reports the stated benchmark outcomes. the research desk inspected but did not execute the implementation or reproduce the values.
mechanism: Across three cycles, a fixed editor helper searches for harness changes while a task model is updated with reinforcement learning; the paper frames the process as recursive co-evolution of the execution harness and task model.
strongest_baseline: The reported headline comparison is the initial task-model/harness system at 42.2% single-attempt accuracy versus 73.3% after three co-evolution cycles; this is an author-reported within-study comparison, not an independent benchmark.
summary: Li et al. describe a recursive-in-recursive process that edits an execution harness and trains a task model over three cycles. On their task-ID-held-out scientific-task benchmark, the authors report single-attempt accuracy rising from 42.2% to 73.3%, with 33.3% of cases changing from incorrect to correct and 2.2% from correct to incorrect. The measurements are author-reported benchmark outcomes, not verified scientific discoveries. The linked repository’s maintained preview uses a different task inventory and experiment configuration from the paper case study, so it does not independently validate those values.
title: ScienceBuddy reports gains from co-evolving a scientific-task harness and language model
why_it_matters: If replicated on independently authored scientific tasks with outcome checks, co-evolving a research execution harness and its task model could improve task completion. The current evidence establishes a bounded author-run benchmark result; it does not show that the system made scientific discoveries or that the currently maintained repository reproduces the paper case study.

demonstrated_result: The inspected arXiv v1 describes the experiment and reports its methods, task cells and result tables. the research desk did not access or independently execute the paper-linked artifacts.
mechanism: MechSparse ranks attention heads and MLP blocks by normalized activation-patching recovery on clean/corrupted task probes, then places QLoRA only at selected sites under a matched adapter budget. MechSparse-C adds a bounded within-layer joint-subset credit. Comparators are random, weight magnitude, activation norm, and gradient/Fisher. The same quantized base model is used during probing and training.
organizations: Ho Chi Minh City University of Technology
Vietnam National University Ho Chi Minh City
strongest_baseline: Activation-norm leads on the headline span+type F1 metric (0.539 versus MechSparse-C at 0.511). Magnitude is statistically unresolved against MechSparse-C in the reported pooled-prediction comparison. The single-seed MT comparisons do not establish a winner.
summary: Xuan et al. test whether activation-patching scores can select LoRA/QLoRA sites better than random, magnitude, activation-norm and gradient/Fisher heuristics. Across three Ministral-8B/NF4 task cells, their causal selectors do not win the primary metric. On the headline three-seed Swahili span-JSON extraction cell, MechSparse-C trails activation-norm by 0.028 span+type F1 (95% pooled-prediction bootstrap CI [-0.048,-0.007]), is statistically unresolved against magnitude, and beats random and gradient/Fisher. The single-seed English-to-Swahili translation cell shows no reliable pairwise separation within 0.30 BLEU. The authors interpret selector quality as task-shaped, but the recommendation to use causal selection on content-dominated tasks remains unproven: no tested cell provides a positive multi-seed result. The study is one model and three narrow cells; probe-based selection costs about 1.7 L40S GPU-hours per cell before reuse.
title: MechSparse finds causal sparse-adapter selection loses to activation norms on schema-heavy extraction
why_it_matters: The negative result cautions against assuming that mechanistic localization improves sparse fine-tuning: a cheap activation-norm heuristic wins the paper's schema-heavy headline metric, while the expensive causal method does not win any primary metric. If the result generalizes, it changes a local adapter-placement choice and the cost accounting for interpretability-guided PEFT. The proposed task-shaped selector rule remains preliminary.

demonstrated_result: The inspected arXiv v1 establishes that the authors published this method and reported the stated tables and setup. the research desk did not execute the code or reproduce the results.
mechanism: A Fast System maintains competing code and skill hypotheses, selects matched physical experiments by expected information gain per estimated cost, and uses outcomes to revise code and skills jointly. A Slow System builds hierarchical memory and trains a policy to select memory actions based on downstream task improvement, uncertainty reduction and experiment cost. The robot foundation model remains frozen during execution; the paper's real-robot setup fine-tunes SmolVLA before trials.
strongest_baseline: The paper reports Harness VLA as the strongest RoboCasa365 Composite-Unseen baseline (40.1%) and LIBERO-Pro baseline (72.1%). For physical tasks it compares the same SmolVLA backbone alone with SmolVLA under EmbodiedRSI's harness.
summary: Song et al. introduce EmbodiedRSI, a harness around a frozen robot foundation model that selects physical experiments by value of information, co-evolves code and skills, and learns which memories improve later adaptation. The 7 October 2026 preprint reports 77.0% overall success on RoboCasa365 and 71.3% on Composite-Unseen versus 40.1% for Harness VLA; on LIBERO-Pro it reports 86.8% versus 72.1%. On a physical SO-101 arm, the authors report 71.3% success across five tasks versus 46.0% for SmolVLA alone, with 30 trials per condition per task. These are author-reported results, not independently reproduced. The physical evaluation is limited to five tasks; the harness lowers success on the glasses-grasp task, and the foundation model is not updated.
title: EmbodiedRSI reports hypothesis-guided harness evolution with transfer to five real-robot tasks
why_it_matters: If the reported gains hold in broader independent trials, choosing informative physical experiments and jointly updating executable skills and code could make robot adaptation more sample-efficient without retraining the foundation model. The reported real-robot evidence is promising but narrow, and does not establish general recursive self-improvement or broad transfer.

demonstrated_result: The official final guideline PDF and MAS release establish issuance, scope, supervisory expectations, phased effective dates, independent validation for high-risk use cases and selected agent monitoring expectations.
mechanism: Financial institutions identify and inventory AI use, assess each use case’s materiality, and apply proportionate lifecycle controls. For higher-risk use cases the guideline calls for independent pre-deployment validation and tested contingency plans. Third-party controls address provider assurance, supply-chain and concentration risks; ongoing monitoring can cover agent reasoning paths, actions and tools.
strongest_baseline: The final MAS guideline and issuance release; the prior November 2025 consultation is superseded for the final policy position.
summary: Singapore’s Monetary Authority issued final AI risk-management guidelines for financial institutions on 7 October 2026. They set supervisory expectations for board and senior-management oversight, AI inventories and risk assessment, proportionate lifecycle controls, and third-party AI; they explicitly include generative AI and agents. For higher-risk use cases, the guideline calls for independent pre-deployment validation and tested contingency plans; relevant monitoring can include agent reasoning paths, actions and tools. The guidelines take effect in phases from 7 October 2027 through 7 October 2028. MAS plans further consultation in 2027 on agentic-AI guidance. The issuance establishes supervisory expectations, not institution-level implementation or observed outcomes.
title: Singapore MAS sets phased AI risk-management expectations for financial institutions, including agents
why_it_matters: The guidelines turn broad responsible-AI principles into a financial-sector supervisory framework for identifying AI use, assessing materiality, controlling the lifecycle, and overseeing third-party systems. For higher-risk uses, independent pre-deployment validation and tested fallbacks add concrete assurance work; monitoring can include agent actions and tool use. The rules are future-effective, so adoption and market effects remain unobserved.

demonstrated_result: Direct inspection confirms that arXiv v1 describes the task and reports these author-run results. This activation did not run the benchmark or independently reproduce them.
mechanism: Agents receive observational data and a six-hour budget to build low-order stochastic ENSO models, freeze diagnostic code and submit outputs. Hidden scoring evaluates statistical properties, reconstruction of hidden variables and forecasts on held-out years.
strongest_baseline: The published reference scores 0.378 overall. Six of twelve final agent submissions exceed it; the paper reports Fable 5.1 at 0.515, Kimi K3 at 0.479 and GPT-5.6 Sol at 0.443. The reference is strongest on statistical matching, while agent entries often do better on reconstruction or forecasting.
summary: A new arXiv benchmark asks AI agent systems to build compact stochastic models of El Niño–Southern Oscillation from observations. The paper reports that six of twelve final agent submissions scored above its published reference overall and that some agent-built models better matched reconstruction or held-out forecast measures, while the reference led on statistical matching. The paper's two model families echo competing explanations of ENSO asymmetry, but do not resolve the physical debate. Results come from one six-hour run per system, with limited single-run access controls; independent reproduction is open.
title: SciExam reports AI agent systems building ENSO models that beat a published benchmark reference
why_it_matters: This is a concrete test of whether agent systems can construct compact scientific models against hidden diagnostics and held-out observations, beyond answering a fixed question. If replicated, it could inform how research agents are evaluated for model building. The reported scores are one-off benchmark outcomes, and the candidate mechanism families are not confirmed discoveries about ENSO.

demonstrated_result: Direct inspection confirms the arXiv v1 paper describes the infrastructure and reports the stated task inventory and experiments. The empirical performance and transfer results remain author-reported.
mechanism: Experts define scientific modules, observables and acceptance policies around pinned repositories. Task factories propose changes; executable validation admits tasks, and verifier-graded interaction trajectories feed evaluation, SFT and RL.
strongest_baseline: Model–harness systems are compared under a common task interface and one-hour budgets; selected SFT comparisons pair initial and tuned checkpoints on the same items. No independent platform or reproduction comparison was inspected.
summary: The arXiv v1 paper describes an infrastructure for packaging scientific codebases with executable checks and generating tasks for agent evaluation, supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning. It reports 64 environments from 27 scientific codebases, 2,812 tasks and 1,076 executable checks. On an 85-task hard subset, 15 model–harness systems received one-hour budgets; the highest reported success estimates were 67.1% for Fable 5.1, 64.6% for Opus 5 and 63.1% for Astra. Fable was measured once and the Opus/Astra intervals overlap, so the paper does not establish a stable ordering. The paper also reports selected supervised-learning gains on held-out scientific-code repair and public benchmarks. These are author-reported results; independent reproduction and broader external validation remain open.
title: ScienceIDE paper reports scientific-code environments for agent evaluation and training
why_it_matters: If the reported environment and verifier approach generalizes, scientific codebases could supply reusable, outcome-checked training experience rather than only static text or hand-built benchmark tasks. The paper demonstrates a substantial computational-science testbed and selected model-learning results, but its current evidence is mostly repair and implementation in computational physics and geoscience, not open-ended scientific discovery.

demonstrated_result: Direct inspection confirms that arXiv v1 specifies the benchmark method and reports the stated task counts and outcomes. The empirical results remain author-reported and were not independently reproduced.
mechanism: The mine–craft–patch pipeline discovers user-visible behaviors in a working reference application, replays them to verify traces, masks source implementations to create repair tasks, then checks whether a coding agent restores the reference behavior. Prerequisite lineages control restoration depth.
strongest_baseline: Within benchmark tasks, agents are compared using shared replay-verified behaviors and reference/current application setup. No independent benchmark or matched alternate-harness replication was inspected.
summary: The arXiv v1 paper introduces ProgramDistill, a benchmark built from 26 interactive web applications. Its automated pipeline reports 1,975 replay-verified behaviors and 4,063 repair tasks. On the paper’s nine-agent partial-application evaluation, success on two leading agents falls as restoration depth grows from 1 to 8: GPT-6 Astra from 100% to 64.0%, and Claude Opus 5 from 96% to 32%. The authors report that this decline persists among runs with similar prompt lengths. These are author-run benchmark results; the benchmark was not independently reproduced and the authors say its public release is still in preparation.
title: ProgramDistill reports a reference-guided benchmark where coding-agent success falls as web-app restoration depth grows
why_it_matters: The benchmark tests a coding-agent demand that issue-based tasks often omit: infer behavior from a working application, then restore it in a partial implementation. If its replay verification and depth controls generalize, it could help distinguish agents’ information gathering and multi-step repair ability. The evidence is confined to the paper’s web applications and experimental harness.

demonstrated_result: Direct inspection confirms the arXiv v1 preprint contains the described method, evaluation protocols, results and internal inconsistencies. The empirical performance and usability claims remain author-reported.
mechanism: A multi-agent workflow generates a mathematical specification from a paper, implements an executable model, then explains its implications. The authors describe a shared first-principles constitution, separate functional and scientific checks, repair loops, and best-of-three selection.
strongest_baseline: Human evaluation of generated artifacts against source papers and paper claims; no matched competing model-generation system or independent replication is reported.
summary: The arXiv v1 paper describes Rosetta, a multi-agent pipeline that turns architecture-paper PDFs into a mathematical specification, executable Python model and plain-English interpretation. In 12 expert-reviewed papers, evaluators rated specification and interpretation quality 4 or 5 out of 5 for 10 papers and reported no significant hallucinations. A six-group author self-evaluation reported concrete paper changes in four cases. The paper also reports a broader 97-paper benchmark result, but its abstract, results section and conclusion give inconsistent denominators and percentages; that result is not summarized as settled.
title: Rosetta paper reports autonomous first-principles performance models that surface assumptions in architecture papers
why_it_matters: If the reported method holds up, automatically deriving auditable performance models could reduce the expert effort needed to inspect hardware claims and expose missing assumptions. The current evidence is one preprint, with small human-evaluation samples, disclosed model-quality failures and inconsistent aggregate benchmark figures.

demonstrated_result: The paper documents its molecule set, reference-energy protocol, coordinate presentation, pair filtering and reported rankings. Its repository exposes data and precomputed responses. This supports the existence of a reproducible benchmark artifact, not independent confirmation of the model results.
mechanism: The benchmark presents rotated Cartesian coordinates and asks language models to rank conformers by relative stability. Reference labels use r2SCAN-3c calculations; ten molecules receive higher-level checks against DLPNO-CCSD(T). The analysis scores reliable conformer pairs and compares model rankings with classical force fields.
strongest_baseline: MMFF94 (mean reliable-pair Kendall τ 0.93), with GFN-FF at 0.72; strongest reported language-model scores are GPT-6 Astra 0.67 and Claude Opus 5 0.61.
summary: Semakin et al. test whether language models can rank molecular conformers from 3D coordinates using relative-energy labels. Their benchmark covers 810 geometries from 27 small molecules. Table 1 reports GPT-6 Astra at mean reliable-pair Kendall τ 0.67 and Claude Opus 5 at 0.61, above UFF (0.23) but below MMFF94 (0.93) and GFN-FF (0.72). The result is a bounded author-run preprint benchmark, not evidence that language models replace molecular mechanics or generalize across chemical space.
title: Frontier language models rank small-molecule conformers above UFF but below MMFF94
why_it_matters: A language model’s ability to rank some small-molecule conformers from coordinates could inform hybrid AI chemistry workflows. The comparison also places the capability in context: in this benchmark, the best tested models trail established force-field baselines, and the 27-molecule regime does not test broad chemical generalization.

demonstrated_result: OpenAI published an Oct 8 report describing two account clusters, its account-enforcement action and the evidence/limitations it used to assess campaign reach. The report is direct evidence of the company's account and assessment, not independent confirmation of actor attribution or every claimed operation outcome.
mechanism: OpenAI says operators used its models for internal campaign reporting and content editing, including drafting or refining articles, pitches, comments, translations and synthetic-media scripts. The campaigns also relied on non-model mechanisms: fabricated outlet/think-tank identities, human intermediaries, false documents, account networks and placement through real publications.
strongest_baseline: OpenAI compares the cases with pre-AI influence operations and its prior reporting on 30 covert operations; no matched comparison isolates how much AI changed cost, output volume, success rate or audience reach.
summary: OpenAI reports that it banned two account clusters it attributes to separate Russian- and Iranian-origin influence operations. The company says one operated a purported Latin American research center and used unwitting local staff, fabricated documents and synthetic media; the other used seven journalist bylines to pitch articles and generated batches of social-media comments. OpenAI says some content appeared in real media outlets, and estimates the Russian-linked operation at category 5 and the Iranian-linked operation at category 4 on the Brookings Breakout Scale. These are company assessments based partly on its account data and open-source checks, not an independent audit of attribution or reach. Spanish-language reporting confirms that related false content circulated in the region, but the reviewed examples do not establish linkage to these account clusters; one superficially similar Ecuador recruitment fake was reported as circulating in 2025.
title: OpenAI reports Iran- and Russia-linked false-front influence campaigns using its models
why_it_matters: If the attribution and operational account are accurate, the cases show AI being used as one part of influence workflows that also rely on fake organizations, human intermediaries, fabricated documents and placement in real outlets. The source says model use was often internal reporting or editing rather than generating the full campaign, and reports exaggerated self-measured impact; that distinction matters when assessing what AI contributed and how much reach the operations achieved.

demonstrated_result: The paper and public OpenVDN repository expose a concrete VDN-H3 architecture, training/inference code and separately licensed weights. The paper’s experiment setup states 103 fixed third-party prompts, H200/B200 environments and automatic video-quality metrics. These artifact and protocol facts do not independently validate output quality or timing.
mechanism: VDN preserves exact softmax attention inside a tokenizer-aligned temporal window and at the first/last latent-frame anchors, while bidirectional frame-wise linear memory handles more distant video context. Video Delta Attention solves one joint regularized update per frame so correlated spatial key/value writes interact; separate gates and output projections calibrate the two branches. A staged adaptation and eight-step distillation adapt the pathway to pretrained MiniMax H3.
strongest_baseline: Dense MiniMax H3 at matched 50 denoising evaluations for the architecture-only single-GPU timing comparison; the paper also compares Radial Attention at matched latency and FastH3 v2 for eight-evaluation quality. Its headline cumulative speedup uses a different one-GPU/50-step baseline than the eight-GPU/eight-step VDN endpoint.
summary: Xi et al. present Video DeltaNet (VDN), a hybrid attention design instantiated on MiniMax H3 for video diffusion. It keeps exact softmax attention within a local temporal window and at first/last-frame anchors, while bidirectional linear memory handles distant video context; a frame-wise joint delta update couples correlated spatial writes. The authors report that, at 50 denoising evaluations on one B200, VDN-H3 reduces backbone latency from 799.6 to 307.9 seconds (2.6×) while remaining close to the dense baseline on their automatic quality metrics. Their optimized eight-step, eight-B200 path reports 6.7 seconds of denoising for a 14.3-second 768p clip. These are author-reported measurements, not independent reproductions; the final speed combines architecture, distillation and multi-GPU inference.
title: Video DeltaNet combines local softmax and linear memory for faster long-video diffusion
why_it_matters: If the reported quality and latency hold beyond the authors’ fixed prompt set, combining local exact attention with compressed long-range memory could lower the inference cost of long video generation without relying on a full dense attention map. The evidence is one MiniMax H3 implementation using high-end accelerators and substantial optimization; transfer to other models, hardware and production workloads is unmeasured.

demonstrated_result: Official Department of Finance pages document publication, scope, assurance cornerstones and mapped practices.
mechanism: A national framework maps Australia’s AI Ethics Principles to governance and risk-based, lifecycle assurance practices for government AI development, procurement and deployment.
strongest_baseline: Earlier jurisdictional government AI guidance and the 2019 Australian AI Ethics Principles; the new framework sets a national assurance foundation while preserving local policy development. NSW’s 2026–2028 strategy says state agencies will comply with its own AI Assurance Framework, illustrating a jurisdiction-level commitment rather than the new national framework’s binding status.
summary: Australia’s Department of Finance published a national foundation for assurance of AI use across Australian, state and territory governments. The framework spans development, procurement and deployment and describes risk-based, lifecycle practices, including governance, testing and ongoing monitoring. It leaves detailed policies to each jurisdiction and says practices should reflect local law and operational context; publication alone does not establish binding force, adoption or outcomes. A 2026–2028 NSW strategy separately says state agencies will comply with NSW’s AI Assurance Framework, an example of jurisdiction-specific commitment rather than a national mandate.
title: Australia sets a national foundation for AI assurance across government
why_it_matters: Government-wide assurance choices can shape which AI systems are procured and how public services test, monitor and govern them. The framework creates a shared foundation, but its effects depend on jurisdiction-specific policy and implementation.

demonstrated_result: The arXiv preprint, its reported experimental analysis and a public code repository are available. Outcome measurements are author-reported and were not independently reproduced here.
mechanism: Sampled-token OPD scores the token emitted by the student. If teacher and student prefer different surface tokens for the same stopping event, the student-native EOS can receive suppressive supervision while the teacher-preferred EOS is rarely sampled. The paper compares decoder stop-set changes with teacher-side mapping, semantic EOS aggregation and canonical-EOS corrections.
organizations: University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill
strongest_baseline: Vanilla sampled-token OPD and a decoder-only shared stopping set; probability-level correction variants are compared on the paper’s fixed setup. TRB arXiv:2605.31159v1 Appendix D already specifies mapping native EOS tokens to one shared stop event, but comparative empirical performance between the papers is not established.
summary: A September 17 preprint studies length inflation in sampled-token on-policy distillation (OPD). It argues that when a base student and post-trained teacher encode the same stopping decision with different tokens, the teacher can give a negative signal to the student’s sampled EOS while the teacher-preferred token receives little support. Across Qwen3, Llama 3.2 and Gemma 3, the authors report that aligning total probability over semantically equivalent stop tokens in the distillation signal reduces mismatch-driven length and clipping; merely expanding the decoder stop set does not. An earlier OPD paper already describes EOS canonicalization in Appendix D, so the basic alignment idea is prior art; the newer paper adds cross-family empirical comparisons, a shared-declared-set Gemma test and stage-wise residual analysis. It also reports late-stage K2-Horizon re-inflation after correction. These are author-run, single-turn mathematical-reasoning results; multi-turn/tool semantics and independent replication remain open.
title: A paper reports semantic stop-token alignment reduces length inflation in on-policy distillation
why_it_matters: Termination mismatch is a concrete implementation-level failure mode that can waste generated tokens and training budget while obscuring whether longer outputs reflect useful reasoning. The basic EOS-canonicalization idea was already described in earlier OPD work; this paper adds cross-family empirical comparisons, including learned preference mismatch despite a shared declared stop set, and documents residual late-stage inflation. The single-turn math regime and remaining failures mean it is not a complete explanation or a general agent-control solution.

demonstrated_result: Official ICO announcement and consultation page document the reported developer commitments, open call, topics and ongoing enquiries.
mechanism: The ICO combines supervision of foundation-model developers with a public call for evidence to inform data-protection guidance for agentic AI and ongoing enquiries into reported testing/deployment incidents.
strongest_baseline: Prior foundation-model supervision and the ICO's earlier general data-protection guidance; this announcement adds reported developer changes and a dedicated agentic-AI call/enquiries.
summary: On 8 October 2026, the UK Information Commissioner's Office said ten major foundation-model developers operating in the UK had made or committed to changes covering transparency, people's ability to exercise their data rights, and safeguards. The ICO also opened a six-week call for evidence on data-protection risks of agentic AI, closing 20 November, and said enquiries into OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta and the UK AI Security Institute concerning earlier testing and deployment were ongoing. The notice does not identify each developer's completed actions, report investigation findings or demonstrate that the changes reduced risk.
title: UK ICO reports developer privacy commitments and opens an agentic-AI evidence call
why_it_matters: The announcement identifies active regulatory work at the intersection of foundation-model privacy, agent autonomy and data-protection law. The consultation may shape future UK guidance, but the public record does not establish implementation quality, inquiry findings or measured risk reduction.

demonstrated_result: The paper reports measured LongBench task scores and effective KV compression for Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen-2.5-7B. The reported system-level latency and energy savings are analytical model outputs for Llama-3.1-8B, not results measured on physical Compute-in-Flash hardware; the research desk did not reproduce either result.
mechanism: Combines integer-only compute-in-flash operations with a flash-resident static dictionary. KV vectors are encoded as sparse codes over the dictionary; attention operates on codes while keeping a recent window in full precision. The design models SSD-CIM compute and memory movement for decode.
strongest_baseline: LongBench compares the combined method to FP16 with full KV cache. System model configuration S2 is compared to B1, an NPU+DDR5 DRAM FP16 baseline with full KV cache moved each decode step; B2 and S1 are additional modeled ablations.
summary: The paper combines integer-only compute-in-flash inference with a static flash-resident dictionary that stores compressed KV-cache codes. On LongBench, the authors report that the combined pipeline retains 99% of the FP16 full-KV baseline score across Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen-2.5-7B, with less than one average score-point degradation and nearly 15× dynamic KV traffic compression. Separately, an analytical model for Llama-3.1-8B at batch size 1 projects 3.1× lower decode latency and 2.7× lower energy at 1K context, and 4.4×/6.8× at 256K, against an NPU+DDR5 full-KV baseline. These system-level numbers are modeled, not measurements on physical Compute-in-Flash hardware; prefill is outside the study.
title: LLM Inference in a Flash reports compressed KV caching and modeled Compute-in-Flash gains
why_it_matters: Long-context decoding can be limited by moving KV state between memory and compute. The paper reports a large reduction in dynamic KV traffic with small LongBench score changes, then models potential decode benefits on a Compute-in-Flash design. The modeled gains depend on assumptions about device bandwidth, dictionary placement and duplicate dictionary storage, and do not establish physical-device performance or prefill efficiency.

demonstrated_result: The paper reports the stated hardware setup, Kimi-K3 rates and baseline comparisons. the research desk inspected the paper's current v1 HTML and fetched the PDF but did not independently reproduce the measurements, inspect runnable code or verify the cited model checkpoints.
mechanism: Stores the full expert pool on NVMe and stages selected experts through host RAM into VRAM. The paper combines fixed-offset expert packs, asynchronous SSD reads and transfers, a three-tier cache, lossless block compression, and CPU/GPU placement selected using end-to-end token latency.
strongest_baseline: Section 5.4 compares against llama.cpp and KTransformers across the three stated model families, and Colibri only on GLM-5.2. The paper reports baseline-specific gains but its abstract/conclusion aggregate ranges do not reconcile with those section values.
summary: The SSD-LLaMA preprint describes an SSD-to-RAM-to-VRAM expert-delivery system with a three-tier cache and CPU–GPU execution placement for MoE inference. On a stated consumer testbed with one RTX 5090, 16 GB host DRAM and a 4 TB NVMe SSD, the authors report running a 2.8T-parameter Kimi-K3 at 1.217 prefill tokens/s and 0.465 decode tokens/s. Section 5.4 reports baseline-specific throughput gains, while the abstract and conclusion give different aggregate ranges; the exact mapping is unresolved. These are paper-reported measurements, not an independent reproduction.
title: SSD-LLaMA reports trillion-parameter MoE inference on a single RTX 5090
why_it_matters: SSD-backed expert delivery may lower the hardware capacity needed to load large MoE models locally, which could change where inference is feasible. The reported Kimi-K3 decode rate is below one token per second, and the paper's speedup ranges conflict across sections, so it does not establish a general consumer-PC performance or cost frontier.

demonstrated_result: The preprint reports +16.7 percentage points on spam at 1B (±4.7 across 39 runs), +21–42 points on spam across four 7–9B architectures, and +13.1 points on SST-2 sentiment in the stated setup. It also reports OLMo/Gemma injection increases with steering magnitude in tested settings, alongside a reduction from 97.5% to 61.1% for 7B Mistral. All results are author-reported; the research desk did not reproduce them.
mechanism: The paper uses Logit Lens convergence to locate where concepts resolve through model layers, then causal head-level attribution to rank intervention points and search steering magnitude. It applies selected activation directions to spam and sentiment classifiers and evaluates both task accuracy and prompt-injection behavior.
strongest_baseline: The paper compares Deep Noir with baseline classifiers, random search and RepE steering without head masking. The authors report RepE matching baseline on SST-2 in the stated folds while Deep Noir improves; the research desk did not verify the statistical analysis or rerun the comparisons.
summary: The Deep Noir preprint combines Logit Lens timing with causal head attribution to search for activation-steering parameters. The authors report gains on spam and sentiment classification across selected 1B–9B research models, including +16.7 percentage points on spam at 1B and +13.1 points on SST-2 sentiment in the stated setup. They also report that steering magnitude and injection success move together in some model/task settings. The paper's own results are architecture- and task-dependent: steering reduces injection vulnerability in one 7B result and reverses direction for two of three models on a sentiment-adapted attack. These are author-reported findings, not an independent reproduction or evidence of an attack on deployed agents.
title: Deep Noir reports automated activation steering and task-dependent injection risks
why_it_matters: Mechanistic activation steering may automate interventions that otherwise require manual layer and magnitude selection. The same intervention can alter how a classifier responds to prompt injections, so accuracy gains and attack behavior need to be measured together. The preprint reports both effects, but its small-model classification regimes and mixed cross-task results do not establish generalization to deployed agent systems.

demonstrated_result: The paper reports closed-form checks and trained-model measurements on ScanAndAdd. The 29x sampling-noise-floor total-variation figure and perfect sample-level metrics are author-reported for this synthetic task; the research desk did not rerun the experiment or independently audit the proofs.
mechanism: Define an independent-update sampler as selecting a write set from per-position distributions and drawing each written token independently. The paper's core argument is that such a product can match a target joint conditional only where the selected coordinates are conditionally independent; marginal distributions do not identify all dependencies in the joint distribution.
strongest_baseline: On ScanAndAdd, confidence-ranked remasking is contrasted with hand-specified write orders designed around task structure. The latter are an achievable task-specific frontier, not a general decoding baseline; the paper also cites PUNT's approximate conditional-independence testing as related work.
summary: The authors analyze independent-update samplers that choose parallel token writes using per-position distributions and sample each selected position independently. They claim that matching the training joint distribution at a step requires the written positions to be conditionally independent given fixed tokens, and that per-position marginals alone cannot certify this condition. On their synthetic ScanAndAdd task, they report confidence-ranked writes with perfect sample-level validity metrics but a generated token distribution about 29 times the sampling-noise-floor total variation. The theorem is conditional on the sampler class; the measured distortion is from one synthetic task and is not evidence that deployed diffusion models exhibit the same magnitude of error.
title: A conditional-independence limit for confidence-ranked parallel diffusion sampling
why_it_matters: Parallel decoding can reduce generation steps, but good token-level confidence or sample validity does not by itself show that the joint output distribution matches the training distribution. The paper gives a precise condition for one class of independent-update samplers and a synthetic example where correctness and distributional fidelity diverge. This can inform sampler design and evaluation while leaving practical scale and transfer open.

demonstrated_result: The authors report overall R@10 0.856, multi-gold MRR 0.653 and accepted-set precision/recall 0.393/0.879 over 1,752 questions, plus approximately $0.02 per question for their hosted DeepSeek-V4-Flash configuration. These are paper-reported results and costs, not independently reproduced.
mechanism: TRACE decomposes a query into corpus-targeted subquestions; fuses sparse BM25, dense, temporal and exact-string retrieval; alternates search and explicit accept/reject/hold review; carries compact memory and replans between subquestions; then merges and reranks documents by cross-subquestion confirmation and recorded rationales.
strongest_baseline: Dense retrieval is the strongest simple overall baseline in the reported table (R@10 0.734, MRR 0.535); graph and agentic systems use the paper’s specified adaptations and ranking protocol.
summary: Bian et al. introduce TRACE, a training-free agentic retrieval system designed for OCR-degraded, heterogeneous historical archives. On HistoriQA-ThirdRepublic, 1,752 French-language questions over BnF-derived parliamentary debates and newspapers from 1887, the authors report overall R@10 0.856 and multi-gold MRR 0.653, above tested BM25, dense, graph-based and agentic RAG baselines. Its components include corpus-targeted query decomposition, fused sparse/dense/temporal retrieval, explicit accept/reject/hold verdicts with deferred re-evaluation, and cross-sub-question reranking. The paper reports roughly $0.02 per question under its hosted-inference configuration and an internal project prototype accessible to 24 researchers across six institutions. These are author-reported results on one corpus; code was not run, and adoption, expert workload, trust and transfer beyond the 1887 French setting remain unmeasured.
title: TRACE reports accountable retrieval gains on one OCR-degraded French historical archive benchmark
why_it_matters: Historical and institutional retrieval needs relevant documents with inspectable paths back to evidence, especially when OCR errors and mixed sources defeat simple search. TRACE reports that orchestration and corpus-aware retrieval can improve document discovery on one French historical benchmark without training a new model. The benchmark does not show that TRACE reduces historian workload or transfers to other archives.

demonstrated_result: The authors report that the symplectic model remained finite in all 192 episodes through 2000 steps, although its physical energy drift reached 7.1 at that horizon. Under unseen repulsive coupling, the factored model reported regime match 1 with nMSE 0.03–0.18 for tested G values, while a non-factored symplectic control had regime match 0. These are author-reported simulator measurements, not independently reproduced results.
mechanism: A symplectic update evolves a learned Hamiltonian and constrains long-run geometry; a separately factorized potential makes force linear in the intervened coupling, so flipping its sign reverses the interaction by construction. Neither mechanism supplies the other behavior.
strongest_baseline: Matched unstructured predictor, physical-energy-penalty predictor, tuned neural ODE, and non-factored symplectic model; the paper also tests stronger relational architectures and domain randomization.
summary: Wang et al. report a double dissociation in learned physical simulators: evolving a learned energy with a symplectic update keeps rollouts bounded for up to 100× the training horizon in tested conservative systems, while an explicit linear factorization of a physical coupling enables transfer to a never-trained sign of that coupling. Each structure alone fails the other target. Matched controls, including tuned neural ODEs, energy penalties, stronger architectures and domain randomization, probe alternative explanations. The paper also maps boundaries: conservation is the wrong prior under genuine dissipation, and an incorrect assumed coupling form can fit the training regime yet fail under intervention. All evidence is from synthetic simulators and rendered observations; independent reproduction and real-video or physical deployment remain open.
title: A preprint separates long-horizon stability from changed-law transfer in physical world models
why_it_matters: Physical world models face different failure modes: prediction errors can destabilize long rollouts, while interventions can expose a model that simply continues the training law. The paper argues those targets require distinct structural commitments and shows how each can fail outside its assumptions. This sharpens evaluation and modeling choices, while synthetic evidence and the risk of prior misspecification limit deployment claims.

demonstrated_result: The primary paper reports a 6.99–8.98 point IoU advantage over rule lookup across three backbones on its held-out benchmark, alongside universal failure to retire one removed rule. These are reported observations in the paper-defined ServiceNow regime, not independently demonstrated by the research desk.
mechanism: CDA discovers rules by editing records and observing resulting effects, stores each rule as a trigger/effect pair, and carries that model across worlds. Revision and addition are driven by unpredicted observed effects; the paper identifies a missing comparison between expected and absent effects as the retirement failure.
strongest_baseline: The Discovery Agent reads relevant rules from the live system for every question and retains no model between questions.
summary: Mishra et al. introduce EnterpriseWorldShift, a ServiceNow-based benchmark with nine tables, 25 baseline hidden business rules and four successive versions that modify, add or remove one rule at a time. In author-reported tests across three model backbones, a Continual Discovery Agent (CDA) that carries and revises an explicit rule model beat a rule-lookup baseline by 6.99–8.98 intersection-over-union points across 600 held-out actions per backbone. Yet none of the three backbones retired a removed rule, despite observing its effects disappear and reading a rule list without it. The result is bounded to one constructed environment with readable rules; it is not an independent reproduction or evidence of production enterprise performance.
title: EnterpriseWorldShift tests whether agents can keep business-rule world models current as systems change
why_it_matters: Enterprise agents depend on organization-specific rules that can change. This benchmark makes silent rule retirement a distinct failure mode: memory helps with some changes but can preserve false expectations when effects stop occurring. It motivates explicit tests for absent expected effects and rule retirement, while the single-platform, readable-rule setup limits transfer.

demonstrated_result: The paper evaluates Gemma 4 31B IT and Qwen3-32B across eight code and reasoning benchmarks, using identical frozen initial pools for Single, fixed-pool LAV and VRR. It reports that VRR improves over LAV in 9 of 16 model-benchmark settings. Table 1 includes negative results (for example -0.61 and -0.27 percentage points), null results (0.00) and positive cells (up to +4.04 points in the shown table). LiveCodeBench analysis reports some recovered correct answers even when every initial candidate was incorrect. These are author-reported results.
mechanism: VRR builds explicit evaluation criteria, verifies and ranks a frozen initial candidate set, and triggers repair when scores are low or judgments remain unresolved. It retains the initial winner, generates a local repair, a runner-up repair and a new-approach solution, screens malformed or duplicate candidates, then re-verifies and reselects under the original criteria.
strongest_baseline: Fixed-pool LAV selection over the same frozen initial candidates, plus a Single first-candidate baseline. The paper does not establish a matched total-token/latency comparison with best-of-N independent sampling.
summary: Tomihari and Ichikawa introduce Verify–Repair–Reselect (VRR), which feeds verifier diagnostics back into generation: after ranking an initial pool, it retains the winner, conditionally creates repairs of the winner and runner-up plus a new-approach candidate, filters invalid/duplicate outputs and reselects under the original criteria. Across two models and eight code/reasoning benchmarks, the authors report VRR beats fixed-pool LAV selection in 9 of 16 settings. Table 1 includes improvements as well as null and negative cells. On LiveCodeBench, the authors report recovery on some problems where all initial candidates were incorrect. These are paper-reported results using the same model for generation, verification and repair; matched total-inference-budget comparison with best-of-N and independent reproduction remain open.
title: VRR uses verification feedback to expand candidate search, with mixed reported benchmark results
why_it_matters: Verifier feedback can describe why candidates fail, not just which candidate ranks highest. Reusing that diagnostic information to generate alternatives could improve test-time search when every initial candidate is wrong. The paper’s mixed results, same-model verifier/generator and missing compute-normalized best-of-N comparison mean the gain should be treated as a bounded method result rather than general evidence that repair beats more sampling.

demonstrated_result: The paper reports 86 successful executions among 107 accepted-paper research specifications (80.4%). Its generated manuscripts received higher average scores than accepted ICLR 2026 and NeurIPS 2025 comparison papers under ScholarPeer and Stanford Agentic Reviewer. These are author-reported results assessed by automated reviewers, not human venue acceptance.
mechanism: ScientistTwo coordinates agents for literature/problem analysis, seed-idea generation, small-subset and full-benchmark experiments, iterative refinement, ablations, manuscript drafting and simulated review. Code changes are executed and candidate methods are compared with accepted baselines before selection.
strongest_baseline: For task completion, accepted papers’ problem specifications and codebases serve as benchmark tasks. The paper also reports AutoSOTA comparisons, but explicitly says the systems use different hardware and metrics and the delta columns are not a head-to-head common-metric comparison.
summary: Nam et al. describe ScientistTwo, a multi-agent workflow that takes research questions and accepted-paper baselines through idea generation, experiments, ablations and manuscript drafting. On 107 benchmark specifications derived from accepted ICLR 2026, NeurIPS 2025 and ICML 2026 papers, the authors report 86 successful executions (80.4%). They report that generated manuscripts scored above accepted-paper averages on ScholarPeer and Stanford Agentic Reviewer for ICLR 2026 and NeurIPS 2025. These ratings come from two automated reviewers, not an independent human expert panel; they do not establish novelty, expert-level discovery or real conference acceptance. The paper also states that its AutoSOTA comparison is not head-to-head because hardware and metrics differ.
title: ScientistTwo reports an end-to-end automated research workflow, with quality claims resting on AI review
why_it_matters: If independently validated, an autonomous workflow that can formulate and test modifications to accepted research baselines could change the cost and throughput of computational research. The current evidence establishes that the authors report a substantial benchmark run and automated-review scores; evaluator dependence, novelty adjudication, baseline fidelity and independent reproduction remain decisive gaps.

demonstrated_result: The v2 paper describes 106 episodes up to 48.23 hours/120 in-game days and 1,439 questions, organized into 381 tasks per hint level. It reports that most vision-plus-language models remain near chance on average accuracy; under full hints, Gemma-4-31B-it reaches 36.2% all-correct and 74.6% question accuracy with noiseless text-only evidence (L-N). Authors report frequent reliance on simple frequency heuristics and difficulty adapting when behavioral patterns change. These results are author-reported benchmark measurements.
mechanism: SimLife simulates multi-character household activity in The Sims 4 with visual observations, game-action logs and generated dialogue. SimLife-BP builds long video chains from days whose actions satisfy explicit temporal or event-based if-then rules, then asks four binary question types—direct prediction, counterfactual, noisy counterfactual and inverse reasoning—at three rule-hint levels. The visual baseline first summarizes video windows into diaries and then answers from concatenated text; text-only baselines receive cleaner structured inputs.
strongest_baseline: Within the paper, modality and evidence-pipeline comparisons include vision-plus-language diary summaries, language-only responses over noisier action-log text (L), and language-only responses over noiseless structured text (L-N), with full, partial and no-hint conditions. The comparison reveals input/evidence effects but does not isolate a general reasoning mechanism independent of those pipelines.
summary: Peng et al. present SimLife-BP, a benchmark for inferring symbolic behavioral patterns from long synthetic household timelines. The current v2 paper describes 106 episodes, up to 48.23 hours and 120 in-game days, with 1,439 question-answer pairs; tasks test direct, counterfactual, noisy-counterfactual and inverse reasoning under three hint levels. Across reported model evaluations, performance depends strongly on the evidence pipeline: most vision-plus-language models remain near chance on average question accuracy, while Gemma-4-31B-it reaches 36.2% all-correct and 74.6% question accuracy with full hints over noiseless text-only evidence. The authors also report shortcutting by frequency heuristics and difficulty adapting when patterns change. These are paper-reported results in scripted Sims 4 simulations with deterministic symbolic rules and generated dialogue, not evidence of real human understanding or deployed household-agent performance.
title: SimLife-BP tests long-horizon behavioral-rule inference in synthetic household simulations
why_it_matters: The benchmark separates long-context storage from the harder task of inferring and revising a behavioral rule when evidence is distributed across time and modalities.
